questions.q: In the 7:42 AM scenario, what three networking-fundamentals details first make the alert worth investigating?
options: An internal source IP, an unfamiliar external destination, and a non-standard port with a steady beaconing interval
A completed HTTP request on port 80 followed by a normal webpage load
A DNS query that resolves successfully on the first attempt
A single ping that returns a normal response time
questions.explain: The combination of an internal-to-unfamiliar-external connection, a non-standard port, and regular beaconing is what flags the traffic as worth a closer look.

questions.q: Why does the analyst check the compromised account's authorization model (RBAC/DAC/MAC) during this incident?
options: To understand the realistic impact — what that specific account can actually access if this is a real compromise
To determine which port the malware is using
To decide whether the traffic uses TCP or UDP
To rewrite the company's compliance framework on the spot
questions.explain: Risk combines likelihood and impact, and impact here depends directly on what the compromised account's access actually permits.

questions.q: Why does the beaconing pattern in this scenario get classified under Chapter 6's attack recognition as malware/C2 rather than a web application attack?
options: The behavior — quiet, regular outbound connections to an external address — matches command-and-control activity, not an injection or XSS pattern against a web app
All suspicious traffic is automatically classified as a web application attack by default
Port 4444 is exclusively used by web servers
Web application attacks never involve any outbound network traffic
questions.explain: The symptom pattern — steady beaconing to an external host — is a hallmark of malware/C2 behavior rather than an injection-style web attack.

questions.q: Why does the analyst document every step of the investigation, even before confirming whether it's a real breach?
options: Compliance frameworks like NIST and ISO 27001 require a clear record of what was found and done, regardless of the outcome
Documentation is optional and only needed if the incident becomes public
Only the final resolution needs to be written down, not the investigation steps
Documentation replaces the need for any technical investigation at all
questions.explain: Chapter 7's compliance frameworks require ongoing documentation throughout an investigation, not just a final summary.

questions.q: According to this capstone, what course comes next in this career path after IT, Networking & Cybersecurity Fundamentals?
options: Windows, Linux & Security Administration
Advanced Databricks & Delta Lake
Terraform & Bicep
The capstone and career course for this path
questions.explain: This course's closing lesson names Windows, Linux & Security Administration as the next course in the Cybersecurity Analyst → Security Engineer path.
